title: In Jewel-Like Paintings, Wiley Wallace Conjures Enchantment in the Desert
description: From mysterious lights and malevolent mists to ghosts and spirits like the Diné’s skinwalkers, the desert has long spawned myths and tales of the
body:
From mysterious lights and malevolent mists to ghosts and spirits like the Diné’s skinwalkers, the desert has long spawned myths and tales of the supernatural. The American West, in particular, is characterized by its vast canyons, plateaus, and mountains, along with the rugged individualism of its inhabitants who make their lives in a landscape many would deem inhospitable. It’s also not difficult to imagine how the atmospheres of powerful monsoons, the unrelenting sun, or the light of a full moon may conjure the uncanny.
Wiley Wallace, who is based in Phoenix, harnesses the magic of the desert in glowing acrylic paintings featuring crystals, enigmatic energy forces, starlight, and specters. His current solo exhibition, Night Bloom at Arch Enemy Arts, features suitably gem-like works that are 16 inches wide at the largest and as small as six by six inches, exhibiting incredible detail.
“Passage” (2026), acrylic on panel, 6 x 6 inches
In dusky desert scenes, figures convene around nebula-like swirls of light and giant prismatic crystals that appear to rise right in front of them. Wallace evokes wonder and contemplation more than fear or trepidation, as if these events have been sought or even summoned. They may also represent portals, perhaps to other spirit realms or phases of life, with their inherent enchantment in the unexplained and the sublime.
Night Bloom continues through August 30 in Philadelphia. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Clay Transforms into Vibrant and Funky 'Habibti' Sculptures by Maryam Yousif
description: Inspired by both the 20th-century funk art movement in the Bay Area and the visual language of the country of her birth, Iraqi-American artist Mar
body:
Inspired by both the 20th-century funk art movement in the Bay Area and the visual language of the country of her birth, Iraqi-American artist Maryam Yousif merges ancient cultural heritage and contemporary playfulness in vibrant ceramics. Born in Baghdad, she immigrated to the U.S. when she was young and is currently based in San Francisco.
Over the past several years, Yousif has developed her signature Habibti figures, which encapsulate the Arabic endearment for “sweetheart” or “darling,” each adorned with a dress of flowers, landscapes, and other shapes. Many of the works shown here were recently on view in the artist’s solo exhibition at The Pit titled Above Earth, Under The Rays of the Sun, which took its title from a curse tablet uncovered in the Assyrian queens’ tombs in the ancient city of Nimrud.

Few materials are as timeless and versatile as clay, which has been used to make pottery and other objects for thousands of years. Just last year, a 3,000-year-old pottery workshop was unearthed by archaeologists in an Iron Age settlement in Iraq. “Clay, as a medium, has a way of connecting us to the past, and in using it, it opened an interest into historical research,” Yousif tells Colossal. “It’s been so rewarding to study ancient objects, learn how to distill what I’m looking at into new ideas, and create my own world and mythology.” 
The artist describes how she’s compelled to follow rabbit holes in her research, from supernatural beings to queens and their gravesites to industry and commerce. She’s particularly interested in the nature of objects as symbolic or representative of places. Having left her first home for an entirely new experience in a different culture, she explores what it means to bring things with us or, indeed, leave them behind.
“Most of the research I’ve delved into takes place in and around Mesopotamia, too, which I’m always curious about since it’s linked to my background and home country of Iraq,” Yousif says. “I feel like working this way keeps me metaphysically connected to a place that I feel essentially far from in many ways.”
Yousif is currently working toward another solo exhibition with Rebecca Camacho Presents in San Francisco, slated for January. A commissioned work titled “Midrib” will also be included in the exhibition Ancient Queenship: Art, Power, and Presence at the Getty Villa starting in February.

title: Milk Cartons and Bottle Gourds Form Sipho Mabona's Tribute to His Late Father
description: Known for his large origami-style works, Sipho Mabona turns his attention to a deeply personal object in a new series: the calabash. The hollowed,
body:
Known for his large origami-style works, Sipho Mabona turns his attention to a deeply personal object in a new series: the calabash. The hollowed, dried gourd is native to tropical Africa and utilized across the continent as a bottle-like vessel for food and beverage. In The Calabashes We Never Drank Amasi From, Mabona translates his familial connection to the functional fruit into vibrant patterns made from recycled milk cartons.
“The starting point for my audiovisual series of works is my childhood memories of my late father’s stories about his own childhood in the rural Eastern Cape of South Africa,” he says. “One memory that was especially close to his heart, and which he often told my siblings and me, was of drinking his favourite drink, Amasi (Xhosa for fermented milk), from calabashes.”
“Dove”
To create the works, Mabona first cut triangular and rectangular pieces from the gourd, which he replaced with colorful, text-laden snippets of Tetra Pak containers secured with equally vibrant threads. Near the center of each piece is a small mirror that reflects the surroundings through a slightly distorted, curved perspective. When up close, viewers can also hear quiet recordings of Mabona’s father, the late scholar and activist Mongameli Mabona, reading his original poems and excerpts of his doctoral thesis on Xhosa cultural history.
Materially and conceptually, the works highlight how the personal and cultural intersect alongside the distinctly South African sense of resilience, one that emerges in the Black population’s upcycling traditions. The artist shares that the series reflects “how growing up and living in different cultural contexts shapes our worldview, and what interactions arise between generations through the transmission of these worldviews and the exchange that comes with it,” adding: 

The works thus represent, on one hand, a juxtaposition of the different ways of life my father and I grew up in, and on the other, a dialogue between my own artistic work to date and his academic work as an anthropologist, in which he studied, among other things, the significance of symbols within his Xhosa culture… (The sculptures) also refer to the fact that calabashes serve not only to store food and drink, but in Xhosa culture are also the resonating bodies of musical instruments (Uhandi), and are used in rituals to communicate with the ancestors, to whom significant spiritual relevance is attributed.

To display the auditory works, the artist constructed cylindrical plinths made from soil, cow dung, glue, and water, an earthen concoction shaped into round stands reminiscent of the rondavel huts in which the elder Mabona spent his childhood in apartheid South Africa. “This is meant to lend the calabashes, with their anthropomorphic forms, a sense of home in an unfamiliar place, within a kind of animist worldview,” Mabona writes.
Find more from the artist, including additional works collaging found materials into rich, symbolic patterns, on his website and Instagram.
“The Calabashes We Never Drank Amasi From” (2024), calabashes, tetra pack, embossed sheet aluminum, nylon thread, cotton, honeycomb cardboard, soil, cow dung, rabbit-skin glue, MP3 player, 105 × 218 × 209 centimeters. Installation view at Kunstmuseum Luzern

title: NYC Names Bryan Joseph Lee as New Deputy Culture Commissioner
description:
News
								The cultural strategist and producer will work alongside curator and commissioner Diya Vij at the Department of Cultural Affa
body:
News
								The cultural strategist and producer will work alongside curator and commissioner Diya Vij at the Department of Cultural Affairs. 
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
            Bryan Joseph Lee (photo Michael Dajour, courtesy NYC Department of Cultural Affairs)
    
		
				
						Cultural strategist Bryan Joseph Lee has been appointed deputy commissioner of New York City's Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA), the agency announced today, August 17.Lee, who will work alongside DCLA Commissioner Diya Vij, enters the post with extensive experience centering marginalized communities' access to and perspectives in performing arts throughout his career. Through his Harlem-based agency CNTR ARTS, Lee has spent the last five years as a consultant and creative producer for several arts organizations, ranging from the With Love Project and the Ghetto Film School to the Lincoln Center and the Brooklyn Arts Council.The news comes just six weeks after NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani approved $323 million in city funding for cultural affairs for the 2027 fiscal year, marking the largest-ever budget afforded to DCLA.

title: Deepen Your Creative Practice at Vermont Studio Center
description:
Announcement
                 Full and partial fellowships available for artists and writers
body:
Announcement
                 Full and partial fellowships available for artists and writers
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            A Vermont Studio Center residency provides artists and writers from around the world with the time and space to deepen their creative practice while building a solid network of mentors, collaborators, and friends. Sessions run for two, three, and four weeks, and include resident presentations, open studios, and an acclaimed Visiting Artists & Writers program. Nestled in the Green Mountains, Vermont Studio Center hosts a global community within a historic, pastoral village. The walkable campus provides private studios, a dining hall, and private rooms in shared lodging along the banks of the Gihon River. Residents can explore swimming holes, hiking and biking trails, and the rural charm of neighboring towns as they expand their creative potential and build a creative community.The fall 2026 open call runs from August 15 through September 30 and will fill residencies from July 2027 to December 2027. Each session welcomes 40 residents of varying mediums and genres at all career levels. All residents receive partial fellowships and 35% receive full fellowships.  Learn more at vermontstudiocenter.org

title: Mary Heilmann, Painter of Irreverent Abstractions, Dies at 86
description:
Obituary
                “My inspiration for art doesn’t really come from the history of painting,” the artist told Hyperallergi
body:
Obituary
                “My inspiration for art doesn’t really come from the history of painting,” the artist told Hyperallergic in a 2013 interview, “it comes from the community of art as it is now.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Mary Heilmann at the opening of 303 Gallery: 35 Years on July 18, 2019, in New York City (photo Sylvain Gaboury/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)Mary Heilmann, a pioneering abstract artist who enjoyed a late-career renaissance after achieving global acclaim in her late 60s, died on Long Island on Friday at the age of 86. The Bridgehampton and Manhattan-based painter had suffered complications from a fall, according to a statement from her studio. Originally a ceramicist, Heilmann shifted course to painting after moving to New York, crafting off-kilter, geometric compositions that put an irreverent spin on hard-edged abstraction. She adopted a technique that allowed neon-bright colors to drip across her canvases in a sly commentary about largely male artists whose self-serious works dominated much of Manhattan’s downtown art scene. Heilmann’s work would later be featured in exhibitions at the Whitney Museum of American Art, the New Museum, Dia Beacon, the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, the Orange County Museum of Art, the Kunstmuseum Bonn in Germany, and Whitechapel Gallery in London.“My inspiration for art doesn’t really come from the history of painting,” Heilmann said in a 2013 interview with Hyperallergic. “It comes from the community of art as it is now, and also popular culture, like movies and music and books and fashion, especially street fashion, not high fashion.”

title: The Architect Shaping a New Chinese Vernacular
description:
Feature
                Pritzker-winner Wang Shu’s design for the Ningbo Historic Museum reconciles China’s nostalgia with its d
body:
Feature
                Pritzker-winner Wang Shu’s design for the Ningbo Historic Museum reconciles China’s nostalgia with its desire for a shiny, avant-garde future.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Ningbo Historic Museum, designed by Wang Shu, in 2021 (photo 钉钉 via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; edit Lisa Yin Zhang/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            NINGBO, China — In May of this year, I took a short trip to Ningbo, China. I was especially interested in going because I knew that Wang Shu, the first Chinese citizen to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2012, built multiple buildings or complexes within the city — the world’s busiest seaport, on the coast of the East China Sea. In contrast to Richard Meier, Zaha Hadid, and other Pritzker winners who rose to prominence late last century and in the early oughts, Wang was not interested in becoming a starchitect. As I was going to be in Ningbo for only two days, I knew that I would be unable to see all of Wang’s projects and settled for one: the Ningbo Historic Museum, completed in 2008. Because of Wang’s work, I knew that I would return to Ningbo before I had even arrived.Wang Shu in 2026 (photo Luca Fazzolari via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; edit Lisa Yin Zhang/Hyperallergic)
